source.title: Towards Utilising a Range of Neural Activations for Comprehending Representational Associations
source.authors: Laura O'Mahony; Nikola S. Nikolov; David JP O'Sullivan

record.tranche_reason: The study compares interpretations of class-output activations at different ranges, using qualitative examples rather than measuring polysemanticity with the original methods.
record.gate_note: The paper cites polysemantic neurons in related work but does not test their prevalence or study InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55, language-model neurons, superposition, or SoLU. The relevant experiment compares maximal and mid-range square-class logits in a synthetic-data classifier. Downstream MID retraining and benchmark performance results are not rows because they report the method's performance, not whether a neuron has mixed meanings.
record.test_reason: The study cites polysemantic neurons in one related-work sentence but does not measure neuron polysemanticity. Its synthetic experiment compares top and mid-range examples of a square-class output logit in a CNN trained on position-biased dSprites. It shows that mid-range examples reveal a spurious position association. That is entanglement of a class concept with a correlated attribute the dataset was built to contain. It does not show a neuron responding to unrelated inputs, and the study never classifies any neuron as polysemantic or monosemantic. This is a related but different construct, so it is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that mid-level logit activations reveal entangled concepts, mislabels and spurious cues that maximal examples miss. They also conclude that their data-curation method MID, which fine-tunes on mid-logit clusters, substantially improves worst-group accuracy on Waterbirds and CelebA without group labels.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses dataset examples selected by class-logit range, including samples near zero, rather than testing the original sources' neuron-interpretation methods or measuring neuron polysemanticity directly.
record.method_sensitivity: The synthetic-data bias level changes the learned representational patterns; the reported qualitative maximal-versus-mid-range comparison is at bias level 0.4.

fits_no_version.finding: In a dSprites CNN trained with bias 0.4, the top-6 square-logit examples are large squares with no position pattern. Random mid-range (near-zero logit) examples include 3/6 non-squares in the left region the model associates with squares.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-maximal (mid-range) activations of a class output neuron reveal spurious-attribute associations that maximal examples hide.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Workshop/Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision
record.problems: The evidence relevant to activation-range interpretation is qualitative and from a synthetic task; no systematic scoring or frequency estimate across neurons is reported. Figure 6 has no textual description of the displayed examples.
record.rows_left_out: MID retraining and benchmark accuracy results in Table 1 and Appendix A.5–A.7 are omitted because they report downstream method performance, not the interpretation of mixed neuron responses.

untested.parts: No test of image-classifier hidden neurons responding to unrelated inputs; InceptionV1 is not studied.
No test of superposition or capacity as a cause.
No test of initialization, regularization or noise as causes.
No comparison of activation functions or architectures for polysemanticity.
No re-examination of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No neuron is classified as polysemantic under different activation ranges or explanation-scoring schemes; only class-output logits are inspected qualitatively for spurious associations.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the synthetic rows to V7. However, V7 concerns whether a neuron counts as polysemantic depending on the activation range examined. This study examines output class neurons, whose concept is fixed by the label, under a deliberately induced spurious correlation. It never addresses polysemanticity. The evidence is qualitative: six images per range on one synthetic model. The MID benchmark results were rightly left out as method performance.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether image-classifier neurons generally respond to several unrelated inputs or examine the cited InceptionV1 neuron.
No transformer language models or token/context polysemanticity are studied.
Does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
Does not compare activation functions or architectures for polysemanticity, or test whether it can be reduced without substantial performance loss.
Does not test whether apparently mixed neuron responses resolve into one shared feature or related offshoots.
The study compares maximal and mid-range activation examples, but does not systematically score explanations or estimate how often the classification changes across neurons.

rows.subject: Convolutional neural network for the synthetic shape task (two convolutional layers, three fully connected layers, and a final classifier; no model name stated)
rows.stage_stated: trained on synthetic data with bias level 0.4
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the six highest square-class logit examples.
rows.measure: Visual content of examples selected by square-class logit
rows.baseline: Mid-level examples around the square logit sign change
rows.value: The top 6 scoring images were squares with similar large size; they did not reflect the position spurious attribute.
rows.note: Qualitative comparison with the mid-level range; no prevalence estimate across neurons is reported.
rows.check: Top-6 square-logit examples of an output class neuron. This measures spurious-feature entanglement induced by the biased training set, not polysemanticity, so it does not bear on V7 or any other version.

rows.subject: Convolutional neural network for the synthetic shape task (two convolutional layers, three fully connected layers, and a final classifier; no model name stated)
rows.stage_stated: trained on synthetic data with bias level 0.4
rows.operation_detail: Inspected a random sample of six images near the square-class logit sign change.
rows.measure: Visual content of examples selected by square-class logit
rows.value: Three of the six shapes were not squares but were located in the biased region (left of the image); the text also identifies counter-spurious squares among the examples.
rows.note: The paper uses this qualitative contrast to argue that looking beyond maximal activations reveals associations not apparent in the top examples.
rows.check: Mid-range square-logit examples (3/6 non-squares in the left region) show a dataset-induced spurious association, not a neuron counted as polysemantic. The study never scores or classifies neurons as polysemantic, so the row cannot show V7's effect.

rows.subject: Convolutional neural network for the synthetic shape task (two convolutional layers, three fully connected layers, and a final classifier; no model name stated)
rows.stage_stated: trained on synthetic data with bias level 0.9
rows.operation_detail: Displayed maximal and mid-level square-class logit examples.
rows.measure: Displayed input examples at two activation ranges
rows.value: Figure 6 shows maximal and mid-level examples; the text does not describe their content.
rows.note: The paper states that the figure shows the two ranges for a model trained with harmful bias, but gives no textual interpretation of the examples.
rows.check: Figure 6 at bias 0.9 has no textual description of its content. The construct is the same spurious-association lens, not polysemanticity.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The top and mid-level square-class examples show different visible associations, supporting the claim that the examined activation range affects the interpretation (R1, R2).
